newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Site of Florida massacre keeps its secrets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Site of Florida massacre keeps its secrets.

text.p: On the drive through the swamp and cypress country of rural north Florida, a small green sign on State Road 24 says simply "Rosewood."

But Rosewood has barely existed since 1923, when marauding whites torched the mostly black village, lynched some of its citizens and quickly buried their victims. The story is retold in the movie "Rosewood" directed by John Singleton (Boyz N The Hood), which opened last week. But much of the Singleton version is fictionalized.
"Nobody's ever going to figure out what really happened here. And Lord knows I've seen 'em all try," said Christy Thompson, who lives in one of a cluster of trailer homes.

Just one house remains, the former home of white storekeeper John Wright and the only dwelling spared in 1923. A path through the woods marks where the railroad used to run. The cemetery is abandoned. People say the victims were buried there but even that is far from certain.

Thompson is white, as are all her neighbours. More than 70 years later, blacks still have not come back. When she moved here in 1972, Thompson heard a few rumours about the massacre but it was not something people talked about. But hundreds of people came though asking questions, she said, sitting in a porch chair and scratching her dog under the ear.
"They'll see a big tree and decide that was the hanging tree. And every one of 'em looks at us like we was the ones that did it. ... And anybody's alive now was a little child then."
Even a state-sponsored study by three universities in 1993 failed to determine how many died or what happened to ignite the siege and manhunt that became the Rosewood massacre.
MASSACRE WHILE A NATION WATCHED

Yet unlike many race crimes of that era, the whole country followed events in Rosewood as they unfolded. Stories ran in The New York Times and other big dailies. Many papers wrote editorials -- in the North, condemning it, in the South, for the most part, regretting it but ultimately pardoning it.

Some things are known. Rosewood was not as prosperous in 1923 as Singleton depicts it. The sawmill had moved to nearby Sumner, an all-white town, and Rosewood townswomen took in laundry for labourers in Sumner and their families to make ends meet. But it remained a viable community of more than 350 people, with two churches, a schoolhouse and a masonic lodge.

And unlike most communities of their day, Rosewood and Sumner had always managed a peaceful co-existence. All that changed on Jan. 1, 1923, when Fannie Taylor, a 23-year-old white housewife in Sumner, ran screaming from her house. Badly bruised, she said a black man had assaulted her.

Today survivors and descendents of Rosewood families believe Taylor had a white boyfriend who beat her and lied about the black intruder to keep the truth from her husband. At the time, suspicion immediately fell on a black convict, Jesse Hunter, who had just escaped from a nearby chain gang.

Sheriff Bob Walker formed a posse and headed for Rosewood, where they threatened the first black man they questioned with lynching because they did not like his answers. The second man they questioned, a 45-year-old blacksmith named Aaron Carter, was lynched and shot, his body left on a road as a warning.
MOB ATTACK
Next, the mob laid siege to the home of Sarah Carrier, whose family had gathered there, fearing the worst.

"Sarah Carrier was responsible for bringing into the world many of those white men in the mob," said Arnett Doctor, her great-grandnephew and a consultant on the film. "She was a midwife. She also did domestic work. So many of those people knew her personally and supposedly respected her."

The posse grew to as many as 300, many of them men from nearby towns. The first two white men who tried to enter the house were shot and killed by Carrier's son, Sylvester. The other whites then opened fire on the house for several hours until they ran out of ammunition.

Most of the blacks in the house used the lull to escape but Sarah and Sylvester Carrier both died in the assault. The whites then torched buildings and used bloodhounds to pursue blacks in the swamps, where many huddled in the cold wearing only the nightclothes they had on when they fled.

"It was cold. Man it was cold," Minnie Lee Langly, a Rosewood survivor, said before her death last December. "Jesus, I will never forget that day. And them crackers was moving backwards and forwards on the road. All our homes -- they burned every house in that town -- churches and everything. They left nothing -- took all our chickens and cows and everything from us."

By the time they called off the hunt, a week after Taylor first called for help, every black in Rosewood was gone. Those who survived were helped by sympathetic whites who smuggled them onto a train that passed through town.

The official death count stood at eight including the two whites killed outside the Carrier home, but the actual numbers were never determined. One news report mentioned 18 bodies and one white marauder bragged of burying 17 by himself.
When the state of Florida began investigating monetary claims by the families 70 years later, both black and white survivors talked of mass graves but none was ever found.

The claim for damages was based on the fact that Florida's governor was aware of the mayhem throughout the ordeal but did nothing to stop it. The state legislature eventually awarded survivors and descendants $150,000 each -- the only time in U.S. history that reparations were paid to victims of mass racial violence.
